questions.q: What is the distance between the centre of a circle and any point on the circle called?
questions.a: The radius

questions.q: Points X, Y and Z are 3.5 cm, 4 cm and 4.5 cm away from a point P. A circle of radius 4 cm is drawn with centre P. Which of the three points lie on the circle?
questions.a: Y only

questions.q: Points P and Q are marked 5 cm apart, and M is the point on PQ exactly halfway between them. Riya wants ONE circle that passes through both P and Q. Which choice of centre and radius gives such a circle?
questions.a: Centre M with radius 2.5 cm, because P and Q are both 2.5 cm from M

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To get all the points that are 3 cm from a point P, a compass works better than marking points one by one with a ruler.
Reason (R): With the pointed tip kept fixed at P and the opening kept at 3 cm, the pencil passes through every point that is 3 cm from P.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the radius of a circle? (b) Sunita opens her compass against a ruler so that the pointed tip and the pencil tip are 3.5 cm apart, and draws a circle. What is the radius of her circle?
questions.a: (a) The radius is the distance between the centre of the circle and any point on the circle. (b) The radius is 3.5 cm, the gap between the two tips of the compass.
s: States that the radius is the distance from the centre to any point on the circle
Gives the radius as 3.5 cm, equal to the compass opening

questions.q: True or False: On a circle of radius 6 cm, a point at the top of the circle and a point at the bottom of the circle are both exactly 6 cm from the centre. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. Every point on a circle is at the same distance from its centre, and that distance is the radius, 6 cm, whichever direction the point lies in.
s: States the verdict True
Reason: all points of a circle are the radius (6 cm) away from the centre, in every direction

questions.q: Points P and Q are marked 6 cm apart. (a) A circle of radius 6 cm is drawn with centre P. Does it pass through Q? Give a reason. (b) A circle of radius 4 cm is drawn with centre Q. Does it pass through P? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Yes. Q is 6 cm from P, and every point 6 cm from P lies on this circle. (b) No. P is 6 cm from Q, but every point of this circle is only 4 cm from Q, so P lies outside it.
s: (a) Yes, because QP = 6 cm equals the radius of the circle centred at P
(b) No, because PQ = 6 cm is not equal to the radius 4 cm of the circle centred at Q

questions.q: On a wide chart, Arjun draws a circle with his compass open at 4 cm and the tip at point P near the left edge. Zoya uses the same compass, still open at 4 cm, with the tip at point Q near the right edge, 15 cm from P. Arjun says, 'We used the same opening, so we have drawn the same circle.' (a) Is he right? (b) What is the same about the two circles? (c) Does point P lie on Zoya's circle? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) He is not right. A circle is all the points that are the radius away from its centre, so its place depends on its centre as well as its radius; the centres P and Q are different points 15 cm apart, so these are two different circles. (b) Only their size is the same: both have radius 4 cm. (c) No. Every point of Zoya's circle is 4 cm from Q, but P is 15 cm from Q.
s: (a) Not right: a circle is fixed by its centre and its radius, and the centres P and Q are different
(b) Only the size (radius 4 cm) is the same
(c) No, P is 15 cm from Q, not 4 cm, so it is not on her circle

questions.q:
Class 6 students are making a paper clock. Each student marks the centre O, marks the 12 hour points all 5 cm from O, and then draws the dial circle through them with a compass.
(a) What should the gap between the pointed tip and the pencil tip of the compass be?
(b) Where is the pointed tip placed?
(c) Neha first marks four hour points with a ruler. They are 5 cm, 5 cm, 4.8 cm and 5.3 cm from O. How many of these four points will lie on the dial circle?
(d) What must the pointed tip do while the pencil turns?
(e) For an inner ring, every point must be 1 cm closer to O than the dial. What is the radius of the inner ring?
questions.a: (a) 5 cm. (b) At the centre O. (c) Two of them, the two points that are exactly 5 cm from O; the points at 4.8 cm and 5.3 cm are not on the circle. (d) It must stay fixed at O, so only the pencil moves. (e) 5 - 1 = 4 cm.
s: (a) Sets the compass opening to 5 cm
(b) Places the pointed tip at the centre O
(c) Two points: only those exactly 5 cm from O lie on the circle
(d) The pointed tip stays fixed at O while the pencil moves round
(e) Inner ring radius 5 - 1 = 4 cm

questions.q:
For a game in the school ground, the sports teacher ties one end of a rope 3 m long to a pole fixed in the ground and a piece of chalk to the other end. Keeping the rope tight, she walks all the way round the pole and marks a ring on the ground. When the game starts, four children are standing at these distances from the pole: Asha 3 m, Bala 2.6 m, Chitra 3 m and Dev 3.4 m. The nearest point of the boundary wall is 3.5 m from the pole.
(a) In this ring, what plays the part of the centre and what is the radius?
(b) Which children are standing exactly on the ring?
(c) For younger children she wants a second ring around the same pole with every point 1 m closer to the pole. How long should the rope be?
(d) Next year she wants a ring of radius 4 m around the same pole. Can she draw it without the ring meeting the wall? What is the largest whole-metre radius she can use? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The pole is the centre and the radius is the rope length, 3 m. (b) Asha and Chitra, who are exactly 3 m from the pole. (c) 3 - 1 = 2 m. (d) No. Every point of a 4 m ring is 4 m from the pole in every direction, including towards the wall, but the wall is only 3.5 m away, so the ring would cross the wall. A ring of 3 m fits because 3 m is less than 3.5 m, while 4 m does not, so the largest whole-metre radius is 3 m.
s: (a) Names the pole as the centre and the 3 m rope as the radius
(b) Asha and Chitra (exactly 3 m from the pole)
(c) Rope length 2 m
(d) No, because the ring reaches 4 m in every direction but the wall is 3.5 m away; largest whole-metre radius is 3 m

questions.q: Which two properties together describe a square?
questions.a: All the sides are equal, and all the angles are 90 degrees.
o: All the sides are equal, and all the angles are 90 degrees.
Opposite sides are equal, and all the angles are 90 degrees.
All the sides are equal, and the angles may be of any size.
Opposite sides are equal, and opposite angles are 90 degrees.

questions.q: Square KLMN has its corners K, L, M and N in that order around it. Which of these is NOT a valid name for the square?
questions.a: KMLN

questions.q:
For rectangle ABCD, match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. A, B, C and D   2. AB, BC, CD and DA   3. AB and CD   4. angle A, angle B, angle C and angle D
Column II: (p) its angles   (q) its corners   (r) one pair of opposite sides   (s) its sides

A rectangular card 9 cm by 4 cm lies flat on a table. It is turned through a quarter turn, so that its long sides now run up and down.
Statement I: After turning, its sides still measure 9 cm, 4 cm, 9 cm and 4 cm in order.
Statement II: After turning, its angles are no longer all 90 degrees.
Statement III: After turning, it satisfies property S1 (all sides equal).
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A square sheet of paper that is turned so that it rests on one of its corners is still a square.
Reason (R): Turning a shape does not change the lengths of its sides or the sizes of its angles.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) State the two properties, R1 and R2, of a rectangle. (b) Does every square satisfy both of them? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) R1: the opposite sides are equal in length. R2: all the angles are 90 degrees. (b) Yes. In a square all the sides are equal, so the opposite sides are equal (R1), and all its angles are 90 degrees (R2).
s: (a) States R1 (opposite sides equal) and R2 (all angles 90 degrees)
(b) Yes, since all sides equal gives opposite sides equal and all angles are 90 degrees

questions.q: True or False: A four-sided figure whose sides measure 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm must be a square. Give a reason or write the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Equal sides give only property S1. A square must also satisfy S2, all angles 90 degrees, so a figure with four 6 cm sides is a square only if all its angles are 90 degrees.
s: States the verdict False
Reason: S1 alone is not enough; all four angles must also be 90 degrees (S2)

questions.q: WXYZ is a square with its corners in that order and WX = 7 cm. (a) Write the lengths of XY, YZ and ZW. (b) Write the measures of the angles at X, Y and Z. (c) Priya redraws the figure keeping every angle at 90 degrees and keeping XY and ZW at 7 cm, but makes WX and YZ each 9 cm. Which of the properties R1, R2, S1 and S2 does her new figure satisfy, and what is it?
questions.a: (a) XY = YZ = ZW = 7 cm, since all the sides of a square are equal (S1). (b) 90 degrees each, since all the angles of a square are 90 degrees (S2). (c) Her figure has sides 9 cm, 7 cm, 9 cm and 7 cm and all angles 90 degrees, so it satisfies R1 (opposite sides equal), R2 and S2 (all angles 90 degrees), but not S1, as 9 cm and 7 cm differ. It is a rectangle, not a square.
s: (a) XY = YZ = ZW = 7 cm
(b) Angles X, Y and Z are 90 degrees each
(c) Satisfies R1, R2 and S2 but not S1; it is a rectangle and not a square

questions.q: In rectangle PQRS, the corners are in the order P, Q, R, S, with PQ = 9 cm and QR = 5 cm. (a) Write the lengths of RS and SP. (b) Name the side opposite to QR. (c) Rohan writes, 'Rectangle PRQS has SP = 9 cm.' Point out both of his mistakes.
questions.a: (a) RS = 9 cm and SP = 5 cm, since opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. (b) SP is opposite to QR. (c) PRQS is not a valid name, because P to R jumps across the rectangle instead of going to the next corner. Also SP is opposite QR, so SP = 5 cm, not 9 cm.
s: (a) RS = 9 cm and SP = 5 cm using R1
(b) SP
(c) Names both mistakes: PRQS is not an order of travel, and SP = 5 cm not 9 cm

questions.q: Rectangle LMNO has its corners in the order L, M, N, O around it, with LM = 11 cm and MN = 6 cm. (a) Name its two pairs of opposite sides. (b) Write the lengths of NO and OL. (c) Write the measure of angle N. (d) Write two other valid names for this rectangle.
questions.a: (a) LM and NO; MN and OL. (b) NO = 11 cm and OL = 6 cm. (c) Angle N = 90 degrees. (d) Any two of MNOL, NOLM, OLMN, LONM, ONML, NMLO, MLON, for example MNOL and LONM.
s: (a) LM with NO, and MN with OL
(b) NO = 11 cm and OL = 6 cm
(c) Angle N = 90 degrees
(d) Two valid names such as MNOL and LONM

questions.q: To construct square PQRS of side 6 cm, the side PQ = 6 cm is drawn first. What is drawn next?
questions.a: A perpendicular to PQ through P
o: A perpendicular to PQ through P
A circle of radius 6 cm with centre Q
The line joining P to R
A line through Q of length 12 cm

questions.q: To construct a square PQRS of side 8 cm, Sneha draws PQ = 8 cm and perpendiculars to PQ through P and through Q. She marks S on the perpendicular at P with her compass open at 8 cm. Before she marks R on the perpendicular at Q, the compass slips open to 8.5 cm, and she marks R with QR = 8.5 cm. She then joins RS. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: PS is 8 cm but QR is 8.5 cm, so PQRS is not a square, even though the angles at P and Q are 90 degrees
o: PS is 8 cm but QR is 8.5 cm, so PQRS is not a square, even though the angles at P and Q are 90 degrees
PQRS is still a square, because the perpendiculars at both P and Q were drawn
PQRS is a rectangle with sides 8 cm and 8.5 cm
RS is 8 cm and all four angles of PQRS are 90 degrees

questions.q:
Square PQRS of side 6 cm is constructed. Match each step in Column I with what it does in Column II.
Column I: 1. Draw PQ = 6 cm   2. Draw a perpendicular to PQ through P   3. Mark S on it so that PS = 6 cm   4. Join R and S
Column II: (p) gives the fourth side   (q) gives the first side   (r) makes the angle at P equal to 90 degrees   (s) makes PS equal to PQ

Assertion (A): While constructing square PQRS of side 6 cm, once the compass has been opened to 6 cm to mark S on the perpendicular through P, the same opening can be used to mark R on the perpendicular through Q without measuring again.
Reason (R): In a square, the side QR must be the same length as the side PS.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Square PQRS of side 6 cm is being constructed on the base PQ. (a) Why must S be marked so that PS = 6 cm? (b) If S and R were instead each marked 4 cm from P and Q on the perpendiculars, what figure would PQRS be?
questions.a: (a) A square has all its sides equal (S1), so PS must equal PQ, which is 6 cm. (b) It would be a rectangle with sides 6 cm and 4 cm, not a square.
s: (a) All sides of a square are equal, so PS = PQ = 6 cm
(b) A rectangle of sides 6 cm and 4 cm (not a square)

questions.q: Rectangle ABCD is to have AB = 8 cm and BC = 3 cm. AB is drawn, and perpendiculars to AB are drawn through A and through B. (a) How far from B is C marked? (b) How far from A is D marked? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) C is marked 3 cm from B, since BC = 3 cm. (b) D is marked 3 cm from A, because AD is the side opposite BC and opposite sides of a rectangle are equal.
s: (a) C is 3 cm from B
(b) D is 3 cm from A, since AD is opposite BC and opposite sides are equal (R1)

questions.q: Nisha constructs a square of side 5 cm. She draws PQ = 5 cm, draws a perpendicular to PQ through P and marks S with PS = 5 cm. Then, without drawing any line through Q, she opens her compass to 5 cm, puts the tip at S, and marks R where she guesses it should be. (a) Which step of the construction did she skip? (b) A square needs S1 (all sides equal) and S2 (all angles 90 degrees). Which of S1 and S2 can she no longer be sure of? For each one you name, name one side or angle that may be wrong.
questions.a: (a) She skipped drawing the perpendicular to PQ through Q (and marking R on it 5 cm from Q). (b) Both. S1: QR may not be 5 cm. S2: the angles at Q, R and S may not be 90 degrees (any one of these is enough).
s: (a) The perpendicular to PQ through Q was not drawn (or: R was not marked on it 5 cm from Q)
(b) Both S1 and S2, with QR named for S1 and any one of the angles at Q, R or S named for S2

questions.q: On the same base PQ = 6 cm, two figures are constructed on the same side of PQ: square PQRS, and rectangle PQTU with QT = 4 cm (T on the perpendicular through Q, U on the perpendicular through P). (a) Where do T and U lie compared with R and S? (b) Find the lengths UT, US and TR. (c) What kind of figure is UTRS? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) T lies on QR between Q and R, 4 cm from Q and 2 cm from R; U lies on PS between P and S, 4 cm from P and 2 cm from S. (b) UT = PQ = 6 cm (opposite sides of PQTU), US = 6 - 4 = 2 cm and TR = 6 - 4 = 2 cm. (c) UTRS is a rectangle with sides 6 cm and 2 cm: its opposite sides are equal (UT = SR = 6 cm, US = TR = 2 cm) and all its angles are 90 degrees, as they lie along the right angles of the square and of PQTU. It is not a square because 6 cm and 2 cm differ.
s: (a) T on QR and U on PS, each 4 cm from the base and 2 cm short of R and S
(b) UT = 6 cm, US = 2 cm, TR = 2 cm
(c) UTRS is a rectangle 6 cm by 2 cm (opposite sides equal, right angles), not a square

questions.q:
A Class 6 section is making name cards for Sports Day. Each card is a rectangle 9 cm long and 5 cm wide, drawn on chart paper by the construction method: draw the base PQ, draw perpendiculars to PQ through P and through Q, mark S and R on them, and join RS. In one corner of each card the students also construct a square sticker of side 5 cm in the same way.
(a) If PQ is the 9 cm side, how far from P is S marked?
(b) What is the length of RS?
(c) What is the angle at P between PQ and PS?
(d) For the square sticker, how far from each end of its base are the other two corners marked?
questions.a: (a) 5 cm. (b) 9 cm, the side opposite PQ. (c) 90 degrees. (d) 5 cm from each end, since all sides of the square are 5 cm.
s: (a) S is 5 cm from P
(b) RS = 9 cm, equal to the opposite side PQ
(c) The angle at P is 90 degrees
(d) 5 cm from each end of the base

questions.q:
Rectangle ABCD is constructed with AB = 10 cm and BC = 6 cm, the corners in order A, B, C, D. Then point E is marked on AB with AE = 6 cm, point F is marked on DC with DF = 6 cm, and E is joined to F, so that EF is perpendicular to AB.
(a) At what distance from A is D marked on the perpendicular through A?
(b) What lengths are EB and FC?
(c) What kind of figure is AEFD? Give a reason.
(d) What kind of figure is EBCF? Give its side lengths.
(e) Seema wants EBCF, not AEFD, to be the square, with EF still perpendicular to AB. How far from A should she mark E? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 6 cm, since AD is opposite BC. (b) EB = 10 - 6 = 4 cm and FC = 10 - 6 = 4 cm. (c) AEFD is a square of side 6 cm: AE = 6 cm, AD = 6 cm, DF = 6 cm and EF = 6 cm (EF is opposite AD in AEFD), and all its angles are 90 degrees. (d) EBCF is a rectangle with sides 4 cm (EB, FC) and 6 cm (BC, EF). (e) For EBCF to be a square, EB must equal BC = 6 cm, so AE = 10 - 6 = 4 cm.
s: (a) D is 6 cm from A
(b) EB = 4 cm and FC = 4 cm
(c) AEFD is a square of side 6 cm, with all sides 6 cm and right angles
(d) EBCF is a rectangle 4 cm by 6 cm
(e) EB must equal BC = 6 cm, so E is marked 4 cm from A

questions.q: Which of these rectangles can be divided into two identical squares placed side by side?
questions.a: 10 cm by 5 cm

questions.q: In a rough diagram, a small mark '|' is put on two different lines. What does this mark show?
questions.a: The two lines are equal in length.
o: The two lines are equal in length.
The two lines are at right angles.
The two lines will be erased later.
The two lines are the diagonals.

questions.q:
In rectangle ABCD, AB = 6 cm and BC = 5 cm. Point X moves along side AD and point Y moves along side BC.
Statement I: When X is 2 cm from A and Y is 4 cm from B, XY is shorter than AB.
Statement II: When X is 3 cm from A and Y is 3 cm from B, XY = 6 cm.
Statement III: When X is 3 cm from A and Y is 3 cm from B, ABYX is a square.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A rectangle 15 cm by 5 cm can be divided into three identical squares placed side by side.
Reason (R): A compass can be used to transfer a length from one line to another without measuring it with a ruler.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: In rectangle ABCD, X is a point on AD and Y is a point on BC. The length XY when X is at A and Y is at C is the same as the length XY when X is at D and Y is at B. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. In the first case XY is the diagonal AC and in the second it is the diagonal BD. The farthest distance between X and Y is equal to AC and also to BD, so the two lengths are the same.
s: States the verdict True
Reason: the two lengths are the diagonals AC and BD, and the farthest XY equals both, so they are equal

questions.q: A ribbon card is a rectangle 18 cm by 6 cm. (a) How many identical squares of side 6 cm, placed side by side, does it divide into? (b) Ravi says the same card can also be divided into two identical squares placed side by side. Is he right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 18 / 6 = 3 squares. (b) No. Two identical squares side by side need the longer side to be 2 times the shorter side, that is 12 cm, but the card is 18 cm long. Two 9 cm squares would not fit, since the card is only 6 cm wide.
s: (a) 3 squares, since 18 = 3 x 6
(b) No: two squares need a longer side of 2 x 6 = 12 cm, not 18 cm

questions.q: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 10 cm and BC = 6 cm. X is on AD and Y is on BC. Meera measures XY for three positions: X 1 cm from A and Y 4 cm from B gives 10.4 cm; X 2 cm from A and Y 2 cm from B gives 10 cm; X at A and Y at C gives 11.7 cm. She claims, 'If I choose X and Y well, I can make XY shorter than 10 cm.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong. The shortest XY comes when X and Y are the same distance from A and B; then ABYX is a rectangle and XY = AB = 10 cm, as her second reading shows. Any other choice makes XY longer (10.4 cm, 11.7 cm), with the longest equal to the diagonal AC. So XY can never be shorter than 10 cm.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The smallest XY is when X and Y are equally far from A and B, giving XY = AB = 10 cm
Uses her data: the other positions give longer lengths, up to the diagonal (11.7 cm), so XY is never below 10 cm

questions.q: Tara has a paper strip 7 cm by 2 cm. (a) Can it be divided into identical squares of side 2 cm placed side by side, with nothing left over? Give a reason. (b) What is the shortest length she must cut off the long side so that it can be, and how many squares will she then get? (c) How much must she cut off instead to get exactly two such squares?
questions.a: (a) No, because 7 is not a whole-number multiple of 2 (7 / 2 = 3.5). (b) Cut off 1 cm, leaving 6 cm, which gives 6 / 2 = 3 squares. (c) Two squares need a long side of 2 x 2 = 4 cm, so she must cut off 7 - 4 = 3 cm.
s: (a) No, 7 is not a whole-number multiple of 2
(b) Cut off 1 cm to get 6 cm and 3 squares
(c) Cut off 3 cm, leaving 4 cm for two squares

questions.q:
A craft shop sells four border strips. Strip P is 28 cm by 7 cm, strip Q is 30 cm by 6 cm, strip R is 26 cm by 8 cm and strip S is 27 cm by 9 cm. A strip is useful only if it can be cut into identical squares placed side by side, each square with side equal to the strip's shorter side and nothing left over.
(a) Which strips are useful as they are?
(b) How many squares does each useful strip give?
(c) For the strip that is not useful, how much must be cut off its longer side to make it useful, and how many squares will it then give?
(d) To mark the squares on strip Q by stepping a compass along the long side, what compass opening is used?
(e) A customer wants exactly 4 squares from one strip, and the shop may cut off at most one piece from the end of a strip. Which strips can serve her, and which one wastes nothing?
questions.a: (a) P, Q and S, since 28 = 4 x 7, 30 = 5 x 6 and 27 = 3 x 9, but 26 is not a multiple of 8. (b) P gives 4, Q gives 5 and S gives 3 squares. (c) R: cut off 2 cm to leave 24 cm, which gives 24 / 8 = 3 squares. (d) 6 cm, the shorter side of Q. (e) P gives exactly 4 squares with no waste; Q can also serve if 6 cm is cut off (leaving 24 cm = 4 x 6). R would need 4 x 8 = 32 cm and S would need 4 x 9 = 36 cm, which are longer than they are, so they cannot. P is the one that wastes nothing.
s: (a) P, Q and S are useful; R is not
(b) P: 4, Q: 5, S: 3 squares
(c) Cut 2 cm off R to get 24 cm and 3 squares
(d) Compass opening 6 cm for strip Q
(e) P (no waste) or Q after cutting 6 cm; R and S are too short; chooses P

questions.q: Rectangle ABCD has a short side AB = 3 cm and a long side BC = 9 cm. X is a point on AD and Y is a point on BC, and the rectangle is to be divided into three identical squares by two lines like XY. (a) What is the side of each square? (b) Where should X and Y be placed for the first dividing line, and where for the second? (c) How long is each dividing line, and why? (d) Rani places X 3 cm from A but Y 4 cm from B and says she has still cut off a square ABYX. Explain why she has not.
questions.a: (a) 9 / 3 = 3, so each square has side 3 cm, equal to AB. (b) First line: X 3 cm from A and Y 3 cm from B. Second line: X 6 cm from A and Y 6 cm from B. (c) Each is 3 cm, because X and Y are the same distance from A and B, so ABYX is a rectangle and XY = AB = 3 cm. (d) X and Y are not the same distance from A and B, so ABYX is not a rectangle: XY is slanted and longer than AB, and BY = 4 cm is not equal to AB = 3 cm. So ABYX is not a square.
s: (a) Square side 3 cm
(b) X and Y 3 cm from A and B, then 6 cm from A and B
(c) Each dividing line is 3 cm since equal distances make XY = AB
(d) Unequal distances (3 cm and 4 cm) mean ABYX is not a rectangle, so not a square

questions.q: In rectangle PQRS, with corners in that order, which pair of lines are its diagonals?
questions.a: PR and QS

questions.q: A diagonal of a rectangle divides the right angle at one of its corners into two parts. Which pair of angles could be those two parts?
questions.a: 58 degrees and 32 degrees

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about diagonals.
Statement I: A diagonal of a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm divides the right angle at each of its ends into two equal parts.
Statement II: A diagonal of a square divides the right angle at each of its ends into 45 degrees and 45 degrees.
Statement III: In any rectangle, the two parts into which a diagonal divides a corner add up to 90 degrees.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): No diagonal of a rectangle with sides 5 cm and 8 cm divides a corner into 45 degrees and 45 degrees.
Reason (R): A diagonal divides the corners at its ends into two equal parts only when the rectangle is a square.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II for a rectangle PQRS.
Column I: 1. A diagonal   2. The right angles at P and R   3. An arc whose radius equals the length of a diagonal   4. A diagonal splitting a corner into 45 degrees and 45 degrees
Column II: (p) a pair of opposite angles   (q) a line joining opposite corners   (r) shows that the rectangle is a square   (s) fixes a corner that is a known distance from another corner

(a) What is a diagonal of a rectangle? (b) In rectangle WXYZ, with corners in the order W, X, Y, Z, the diagonal WY divides two of the right angles into two parts each. At which two corners are these angles?
questions.a: (a) A diagonal is a line joining two opposite corners of the rectangle. (b) At W and at Y, the two corners that the diagonal WY joins.
s: (a) A line joining opposite corners
(b) The angles at W and at Y

questions.q: True or False: To construct a rectangle with one side DC = 6 cm and a diagonal of 9 cm, a perpendicular to DC is drawn through C, and the corner B on it is marked by an arc of radius 9 cm with centre C. Give a reason or write the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. B lies on the perpendicular through C, so the diagonal from B goes to D, the other end of DC. The arc of radius 9 cm must have its centre at D, not C. (An arc centred at C would make the side CB 9 cm, not the diagonal.)
s: States the verdict False
Correction: the arc of radius 9 cm is centred at D, since the diagonal is DB

questions.q: The diagonal PR of rectangle PQRS divides the right angle at P into two parts. (a) If one part is 25 degrees, find the other part. (b) If the two parts are equal, find each part. (c) What kind of rectangle is PQRS in case (b)?
questions.a: (a) 90 - 25 = 65 degrees. (b) 90 / 2 = 45 degrees each. (c) A square.
s: (a) 65 degrees
(b) 45 degrees each
(c) PQRS is a square

questions.q: Neel tries to construct a rectangle with one side DC = 9 cm and a diagonal of 9 cm. He draws DC, draws line l perpendicular to DC through C, and draws an arc of radius 9 cm with centre D. (a) Which point of line l is exactly 9 cm from D? (b) What happens to the corner B, and so to his rectangle? (c) What must be true of the diagonal compared with the given side for this construction to work?
questions.a: (a) Only C itself, because DC = 9 cm; every other point of l is farther than 9 cm from D, so the arc meets l only at C. (b) B falls on C, so the side BC has no length and no rectangle is formed. (c) The diagonal must be longer than the given side (here, more than 9 cm), since in a rectangle the diagonal is the farthest distance between points on opposite sides and is longer than the sides.
s: (a) Only the point C is 9 cm from D on line l
(b) B coincides with C, so BC = 0 and there is no rectangle
(c) The diagonal must be longer than the given side

questions.q:
A school garden club plans four rectangular flower beds on a scale drawing, each with a straight path along one diagonal. The plans are: Bed 1: the path divides a corner into 50 degrees and 40 degrees. Bed 2: the path divides a corner into 45 degrees and 45 degrees. Bed 3: one side 7 cm and the path 5 cm. Bed 4: one side 6 cm and the path 10 cm.
(a) In Bed 1, the path also divides the right angle at its other end into two parts. What do those two parts add up to, and are they equal?
(b) What shape is Bed 2?
(c) Which bed cannot be drawn? Give a reason.
(d) For Bed 4, after drawing the 6 cm side DC and the perpendicular to DC through C, state the centre and radius of the arc that fixes B.
(e) The club draws every bed that can be drawn. Which beds are drawn, and which drawn bed is a square?
questions.a: (a) They add up to 90 degrees, since the corner is a right angle. They are not equal, because the parts are equal only in a square and Bed 1 is not one (its parts are 50 and 40 degrees). (b) A square, because the path divides the corner into two equal parts. (c) Bed 3. The path is a diagonal, and a diagonal is the farthest distance between points on opposite sides, so it must be longer than a side; here the path, 5 cm, is shorter than the side, 7 cm. An arc of radius 5 cm about D cannot reach the perpendicular through C, whose nearest point C is already 7 cm from D, so B cannot be marked. (d) Centre D, radius 10 cm. (e) Beds 1, 2 and 4 are drawn; Bed 2 is the square.
s: (a) The two parts add up to 90 degrees and are not equal (not a square)
(b) Bed 2 is a square
(c) Bed 3 cannot be drawn: the 5 cm diagonal is shorter than the 7 cm side
(d) Arc centred at D with radius 10 cm
(e) Beds 1, 2 and 4 are drawn; Bed 2 is the square

questions.q: Points M and N are marked on a page. How can a point that is 6 cm from M and also 6 cm from N be found without trial and error?
questions.a: Draw arcs of radius 6 cm with centres M and N; the point is where they cross.
o: Draw arcs of radius 6 cm with centres M and N; the point is where they cross.
Draw one arc of radius 6 cm with centre M; every point on it will do.
Draw arcs of radius 3 cm with centres M and N; the point is where they cross.
Draw a line 6 cm long from M towards N; its end is the point.

questions.q: A House figure is drawn in which every border line is 6 cm long. Its roof point A has been found and joined to B and C. Where is the compass tip placed, and with what radius, to draw the curved arc of the roof through B and C?
questions.a: At A, with radius 6 cm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The point where an arc of radius 5 cm centred at B crosses an arc of radius 5 cm centred at C is 5 cm from B, but it may not be 5 cm from C.
Reason (R): Every point on an arc of radius 5 cm centred at C is 5 cm from C.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: Points P and Q are 6 cm apart. An arc of radius 6 cm is drawn with centre P and another arc of radius 6 cm with centre Q, and they cross at R. (a) Find PR and QR. (b) What do you notice about the three lengths PQ, QR and RP?
questions.a: (a) PR = 6 cm, because R is on the arc centred at P, and QR = 6 cm, because R is on the arc centred at Q. (b) All three lengths are equal, 6 cm each.
s: (a) PR = 6 cm and QR = 6 cm, since R lies on both arcs
(b) PQ, QR and RP are all equal (6 cm)

questions.q: For the House, BC = 5 cm, and arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C cross at two points, one on each side of BC. (a) Why are both crossing points 5 cm from B and from C? (b) Which crossing point is used as the roof point A, and why?
questions.a: (a) Each crossing point lies on both arcs, so it is 5 cm from B (on the arc centred at B) and 5 cm from C (on the arc centred at C). (b) The point on the side of BC away from the square body of the house, because the roof sits on top of the house, outside the square.
s: (a) Each crossing point lies on both arcs, so it is 5 cm from B and from C
(b) The crossing point on the side away from the square body, where the roof belongs

questions.q: Lata has drawn three points A, B and C with AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm. B and C are not on one straight line with A. She wants a fourth point D that is 5 cm from B and also 5 cm from C, to make a four-sided figure ABDC. (a) How should she find D? (b) Her two arcs cross at two points. One of them is A. Why? (c) Write the lengths of the four sides of ABDC.
questions.a: (a) Draw an arc of radius 5 cm with centre B and another arc of radius 5 cm with centre C; D is where they cross. (b) A is already 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C, so it lies on both arcs and is one crossing point; D is the other crossing point. (c) AB = 5 cm, BD = 5 cm, DC = 5 cm and CA = 5 cm.
s: (a) Arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C; D is their crossing
(b) A is 5 cm from both B and C, so it is on both arcs; D is the other crossing
(c) All four sides AB, BD, DC, CA are 5 cm

questions.q:
For a floor design on Children's Day, Meena uses a piece of string 50 cm long as a large compass: one end is held fixed on the floor and a chalk is tied to the other end. She has marked two dots K and L, 50 cm apart, on the floor. She wants a dot M that is 50 cm from K and also 50 cm from L, and then a curved border drawn from M through K and L, like the roof of the House.
(a) What radius should her two arcs have, and where should their centres be?
(b) Where is the dot M?
(c) Where is the fixed end of the string held for the curved border, and why does the curve pass through both K and L?
(d) She wants a second dot N, on the other side of the line KL, that is also 50 cm from both K and L. What centres and radius give N, and why is N 50 cm from both K and L?
questions.a: (a) Radius 50 cm (the full string), one arc with centre K and one with centre L. (b) M is where the two arcs cross. (c) At M, with the string at full length; K and L are both 50 cm from M, so the curve of radius 50 cm passes through both. (d) Centres K and L with radius 50 cm, the same as for M: the two arcs, carried on to the other side of KL, cross there a second time, and that crossing is N. N lies on the arc centred at K, so it is 50 cm from K, and on the arc centred at L, so it is 50 cm from L.
s: (a) Radius 50 cm with centres at K and at L
(b) M is the crossing point of the two arcs
(c) String held at M; K and L are each 50 cm from M, so the curve passes through both
(d) Arcs of radius 50 cm centred at K and L, crossing on the other side of KL; N is on both arcs, so 50 cm from K and from L

questions.q:
Nikhil is drawing a Lantern for the school fair poster. Its body is a square BCDE of side 6 cm, with BC on top. On top of BC he wants a roof made exactly like the roof of the House: a roof point A joined to B and C, and a curved arc through B and C, with every line of the Lantern the same length as the side of the square. His only compass opens to at most 5 cm.
(a) How far must A be from B and from C, and which arcs locate A?
(b) What centre and radius are needed for the curved arc through B and C?
(c) Can Nikhil complete this Lantern with his compass? Give a reason.
(d) His friend suggests keeping the 6 cm body, locating A with arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C (they do cross), and drawing the roof arc with radius 5 cm from A. Will this roof arc pass through B and C? Does this plan give the Lantern he wanted? Decide, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) 6 cm from both B and C, since AB and AC must equal the side; A is where an arc of radius 6 cm centred at B crosses an arc of radius 6 cm centred at C. (b) Centre A and radius 6 cm, since A is 6 cm from both B and C. (c) No. The roof arc must have centre A and radius 6 cm, so the compass must open to 6 cm, but it opens to at most 5 cm. (A itself could be found with a ruler by trial and error, but the arc cannot be drawn.) (d) The roof arc will pass through B and C, because A is then 5 cm from both. But the plan does not give the Lantern he wanted: AB, AC and the arc radius are 5 cm while the sides of the body are 6 cm, so the lines are no longer all equal.
s: (a) 6 cm from B and C; arcs of radius 6 cm centred at B and at C
(b) Centre A, radius 6 cm
(c) No: the roof arc needs radius 6 cm, more than the 5 cm limit
(d) The arc passes through B and C (A is 5 cm from both), but roof lines 5 cm and body 6 cm are unequal, so it is not the wanted Lantern

questions.q:
In a House figure, BC = 5 cm is the top side of the square body BCDE, which lies below BC. Four students try to locate the roof point A, 5 cm from both B and C. Their points measure: Arun: 5.0 cm from B and 5.0 cm from C, above BC. Bina: 5.0 cm from B and 4.6 cm from C. Charu: 4.8 cm from B and 5.2 cm from C. Dinesh: 5.0 cm from B and 5.0 cm from C, but below BC.
(a) Whose points are 5 cm from both B and C?
(b) Whose point can be used as the roof point A? Why not the other one?
(c) Bina and Charu slid a ruler around until the point looked right. Which method avoids this trial and error?
(d) Why is the point given by that method sure to be 5 cm from both B and C?
(e) Who must draw new arcs, and what should Dinesh do instead? (Dinesh drew full circles of radius 5 cm around B and C.)
questions.a: (a) Arun's and Dinesh's. (b) Arun's, because the roof must sit above BC; Dinesh's point is below BC, inside the square body of the house. (c) Drawing arcs of radius 5 cm with centres B and C and taking their crossing point. (d) The crossing point lies on both arcs, so it is 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C at the same time. (e) Bina and Charu must draw new arcs: two arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C. Dinesh needs no new arcs: his two circles also cross at a second point above BC, and he should take that point as A.
s: (a) Arun and Dinesh
(b) Arun's point, since Dinesh's lies below BC inside the square body
(c) Arcs of radius 5 cm centred at B and C, taking the crossing point
(d) The crossing lies on both arcs, so it is 5 cm from both
(e) Bina and Charu draw two 5 cm arcs from B and C; Dinesh uses the other crossing of his circles, above BC

questions.q: A badge called 'Twin Roofs' is drawn on a base line BC = 8 cm, with M the point on BC that is 4 cm from B. Two small roofs are built like the roof of the House: point A1 is 4 cm from both B and M, and point A2 is 4 cm from both M and C, both above BC. (a) State the centres and radius of the arcs that locate A1. (b) State the centres and radius of the arcs that locate A2. (c) Find A1M and A2M. (d) State the centre and radius of the curved arc for the first roof, and the two points it passes through.
questions.a: (a) Arcs of radius 4 cm centred at B and at M. (b) Arcs of radius 4 cm centred at M and at C (MC = 8 - 4 = 4 cm). (c) A1M = 4 cm and A2M = 4 cm, since each point was found on an arc of radius 4 cm centred at M. (d) Centre A1, radius 4 cm; it passes through B and M.
s: (a) Radius 4 cm, centres B and M
(b) Radius 4 cm, centres M and C
(c) A1M = A2M = 4 cm
(d) Centre A1, radius 4 cm, passing through B and M
